text:
Training many machine learning models and averaging their predictions can improve performance, but using a whole ensemble of models is cumbersome and computationally expensive for deployment to a large number of users [P3_p1_c02]. Training large neural networks on very big datasets also requires excessive computation at training time [P3_p5_c04]. 

To solve this, the paper uses a transfer training method called distillation [P3_p1_c03]. The main idea is to compress the knowledge from a large ensemble of models into a single, smaller model that is much easier to deploy [P3_p1_c02]. This separates the heavy computation needed during training from the strict speed and resource limits needed when deploying to users [P3_p1_c03]. 

The paper also introduces a new type of ensemble made of full models and specialist models [P3_p1_c02]. These specialist models learn to distinguish fine-grained classes that the full models confuse, and they can be trained rapidly and in parallel [P3_p1_c02]. 

Regarding key results, the authors achieve surprising results on MNIST and significantly improve the acoustic model of a heavily used commercial system by distilling an ensemble into a single model [P3_p1_c02]. A single model trained this way works significantly better than a model of the same size learned directly from the same training data [P3_p4_c03]. Furthermore, using soft targets allows a speech model with 85M parameters to be trained with only 3% of the data, which is about 20M examples [P3_p7_c03]. While hard targets lead to severe overfitting with this small amount of data, training with soft targets recovers almost all the information in the full training set, ending up about 2% shy without needing early stopping [P3_p7_c03]. The sources do not mention other limitations beyond the high computation requirements of standard ensembles during training and testing [P3_p1_c02][P3_p5_c04].
